en: General Preface to the Commentary and Singing of the Ancient Verses by Linquan Luren on Touzi and Danxia:

Throughout ancient and modern times, those who have offered *niansong* (critical commentaries and verses) on ancient cases have not been few. Yet, among the monastic communities, it is known that only four families [of masters] have mastered this art.

I humbly observe the altruistic intent of these former enlighteners: they employed the public cases of the ancients to guide the masses of deluded beings toward awakening. Thus, they established the "traps" (*shuan*).
May this cause one to swiftly capture the fish and the rabbit within the ocean of awakening and the garden of its nature.

Is this not precisely like the coming of Bodhidharma from the West, who did not establish written words yet was not separate from them? Recently, following along with these attendant monks has brought calamity upon the forests and springs.
In the midst of empty valleys, they insist on transmitting sounds; within the halls of emptiness, they forcibly practice listening. Through this speaking of that which cannot be spoken...
To speak of that which is spoken is to hear what is not heard, yet it is to hear within hearing itself.
I do not presume to join ranks with the Buddha or with Wansong in this world, nor do I dare to vie alongside them; rather, I merely attempt to mimic their expressions.
On the Zhongyuan day of the year Yyou of the Zhiyuan era, the old monk Linquan spoke this for Congyan Mingquan Wujie.

The Elder Linquan’s Commentary and Chanting on Master Toudi Qing’s *Collected Verses on Ancient Cases*,
Volume One. Read by the junior student Xingyi.
The First Case of Master Shengsheng Daoren, Zizhi: Qingyuan’s Stages of Realization.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "Completely forgetting the affairs of the human world—why deliberate thrice? Smash the mass of doubt; what need is there for a single phrase? Not so.
Stuck at the profound pass: who is it that attains the wondrous through both horizontal and vertical movement?
Master Si raised this question for the Sixth Patriarch, asking: "What should one apply oneself to in order to avoid falling into stages?
(If you can simply do good deeds, why must you ask about your future? The Patriarch said: "What have you been doing? (This cuts open the belly and gouges out the heart. Si replied: "The Holy Truth."

[The Master] also did not [grant him] "a single grain of elixir that transforms iron into gold. The Patriarch asked, "In what rank does he fall? [Baizhang] said, "[He acts] like one who hangs down a single hand, not sparing even his two eyebrows.

[Huangbo] thought, "If even the Noble Truths are not employed, in what rank does he fall? [He replied], "When deluded, the triple world exists; upon awakening, the ten directions are empty. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is.
You must protect and uphold this well. I shall have a verse for you. [Huangbo] said, "I wish to hear the essentials of the Dharma. The Mind-ground contains all things.
The seeds are all contained within; a universal rain causes them all to sprout. Having suddenly awakened to the nature of the flower, one does not produce further branches or trailing vines.
The fruit of Bodhi is naturally attained—know that its sweetness comes from amidst bitterness.

The Master said: "The gradual stages of cultivation have been thus throughout the past and present. While it is indeed difficult for those of sharp and dull faculties to be equal, from the stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, up to the levels of Heat, Summits, Patience, the Worldly First Dharma, and the two types of enlightenment—Equal and Wonderful—all do not transcend the mysterious gate of transformative construction responding to the perfect capacity.
To reveal the truth with full sincerity: the realization of the body of wisdom does not come through awakening by means of another. This begins with the initial aspiration."
At that moment, he immediately realized Bodhi. Yet, if one examines it closely, he has only spoken half of it.
Only when one reaches the realization that "the Tathāgata neither appears in the world nor enters Nirvāṇa" does it become eighty percent complete.
As for that single phrase of "ten-part completion," how should one speak of it? A talkative monk finds it difficult to express; the wordless child excels at its proclamation. —Nanyue.
Master Let once said to Master Ma: "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground is like planting seeds;

my teaching of the essential Dharma is like the rain from heaven. Because your conditions have converged, you shall perceive the Way. Furthermore, these seeds are possessed by every person; each and every one lacks nothing.
Be careful not to辜负 (gu fu—disappoint) your own spiritual nature or to bury and lose your family treasure. Having attained his seat, he donned [his robes].
He turned his robe back and looked at it himself. "Though this is a shallow matter from the mouth of a forest spring, you all must not be arrogant or overconfident.

Whether you see it or not, you must further consult Touzi before you can be certain. He then spoke in verse: The robe is turned back; The mind is already clear. If you wish to know the source, You must ask Touzi.

The crown of the head cannot be seen, as clouds gather in haste (to look upon it is to go blind). The numinous branch beyond the kalpas bears no spring (where the three lights do not shine, there is a different way of contemplating).

Not sitting in the palace of the Empty King over there (one cannot remain within the realm of non-outflows), How could one be willing to till the fields toward the solar disk (it would be difficult to see him within the shadows of the moon’s radiance)?

The Master cites the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, saying: "For example, just as empty space pervades all places, whether material or immaterial, yet neither reaches them nor fails to reach them. Why? Because empty space has no body.
The body of the Tathāgata is also like this: it pervades all places, all sentient beings, all phenomena, and all lands. Why?"
Because this coming body has no body, it manifests its form for the sake of sentient beings. Take, for instance, the invisible crown of the head:
how could one possibly grope for it? If the clouds of delusion are dense and the mists of confusion are thick, then even where you must exert your eyes, there is no connection to be found.
How much more so before the empty kalpa—when the spiritual branch flourished of itself without relying on the faculty of thought; what need was there then for the warmth of spring?
As for those who rank and grade [beings], they are originally faceless fellows who have transcended the emotions of gain and loss and emerged from the nest of rising and falling;
neither sages nor ordinary people can fathom them, and their sequence is difficult to constrain. They remain carefree, detached, and perfectly composed.
Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that Nanquan said, "Even Weyinwang Buddha was still but a child of Old Master Wang."
"Grandson. Why? Since antiquity, the wheel-turning kings have possessed complete majesty; they did not need to display their precious seals to be naturally honored.
Second, it is not merely that Caoxi told the assembly:

"To distinguish old from young, to discern the beautiful from the ugly—the refined mirror cannot be deceived; to calculate lightness and heaviness, to weigh the high and the low—there is none [who can do so]."

The Star-Balance emerges. Since it is known that the left eye weighs half a catty, one might expect the right eye to weigh eight taels. Fearing that he would not believe it, [the Master] deliberately examined him in detail.
He brought Shitou to the place of Master Si (a journey made with no small difficulty). Si asked, "Where have you come from? (To discern the field, one examines the seedlings.)
Dongshan said, "From Caoxi" (much talk is not as good as little substance). Nanquan then held up his whisk and said, "Was there this very thing at Caoxi?
(speaking well words in action). Dongshan said, "Not only was it absent at Caoxi; it was also absent in the Western Heavens" (denying it right in one's face).
Nanquan said, "Have you perhaps been to the Western Heavens? (do not pursue the thief further). Dongshan said, "If I had gone, there would have been. (a sweet melon, stem and all).
Sweet. Xingshan said, "I have not yet finished; speak further. (This was to suppress and drive him to his death. Touzi said, "Do not rely on me alone;
you, Master, must also say half of it. (To yield is to have plenty. Xingshan said, "I do not refuse to tell you, but I fear that later there will be no one to take it up.
(He secretly pulls out the cross-bone while sitting openly on the tongue.)
The Master said: "When the Chan Master Xituan of Shitou on Mount Nanyue was a śrāmaṇera, the Sixth Patriarch was about to pass away.
He asked, 'After the Master has passed on, I do not know whom Xituan should rely upon. The Patriarch replied, 'Seek it out for yourself.
When the Patriarch entered parinirvāṇa, Xituan would often sit upright in a quiet place, as still and silent as if he had forgotten his very birth. The First Seat asked him:"
"The Master has already passed away; what is the use of sitting here in vain? [Nanquan] said, "I am following his final instructions, which is why I am searching for him.

[Baizhang] said, "You have a senior brother, Master Si, who currently resides at Qingyuan in Jizhou. Your karmic connection lies there. Nanquan remarked, "The Master’s words were very direct; you are simply deluded yourself.
Upon hearing these words, Xuanzang bowed and took his leave of the ancestral shrine, proceeding directly to the place of Master Si to pay his respects. He then asked him:
"From where have you come? [The Master] replied, "From Caoxi. Mazu held up his whisk and said, "Is there such a thing as this at Caoxi?
Although this was like hanging a goat's head to sell dog meat, he fortunately encountered one who knew the trade; yet he could not frighten him away.

Mazu was countered by him with the words, "Not only is it not at Caoxi, but it is not even in the Western Heavens. This is what is called "avoiding the full expression"; in the pivot of the teaching, subtlety is prized.
"To turn it around. He pushed him toward a ten-thousand-fathom precipice, saying, "Have you come from the Western Heaven?
This may also be appreciated as a case of personal skill and discerning vision. If he had arrived, then [the Way] would exist; yet seeing the matter, he did not understand how to engage with it.
He also said, "It is not yet here—speak further! Thus, Shitou used the opponent's own stratagem against them, saying, "Do not rely entirely on me, O Monk."
One must also speak half of it; seeing that victory and defeat cannot be distinguished, he used sweet words and pleasant speech to entice those who were hungry.

Eihe! The minds of the ancients were like clear mirrors, and their mechanisms were like rolling pearls; they were able, in the midst of question and answer, to forge worldly dharmas and Buddha-dharmas into a single whole.
Is this not what it means to be in profound accord with the principles of the Buddhas? During the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, the Master...
Initially, he retired to the Southern Monastery on Mount Heng. To the east of the monastery was a rock shaped like a terrace;
he built a hut upon it and was consequently known as Master Shitou (Stonehead). A monk once asked, "What is liberation?
He replied, "Who bound you? He asked, "What is the Pure Land? He replied, "Who defiles you? He asked, "What is nirvana? He replied, "Who will..."
He bestowed the cycle of birth and death upon you. Observe how he opened the way for later students, cutting directly to the root with words devoid of branches and leaves;
it is only natural that he is regarded as the patriarch of the Caodong school. As stated in his *Cantong qi*:
"When there is light within, do not meet with darkness; when there is darkness within, do not look upon light. Thus spoke the old man Shitou.
Although this is half-concealed and half-revealed, when descendants and later generations arrive here, how will they respond? The verse says:
White clouds conceal the royal phoenix (not letting people see it makes it all the more elegant). The red sun shines upon the vast void (a separate realm of heaven).
Where the stars cluster in obscurity (beyond the reach of upward gazing), Impartiality presides over the Nine Heavens (so lofty that even its mark cannot be seen).
The Master said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a vermilion phoenix soaring into the heavens, leaving no trace behind.

This arises because the nature is empty and vast, and the sun of wisdom is brilliant and clear. It illuminates that the five aggregates are all empty, causing all myriad conditions to vanish together.

One reaches the point where stars cluster in the azure void and the moon bathes the vermilion steps; the emerald curtains hang down, the incense burns, and all is still. At such a moment, how [could there be anything else]?"
Allow me to catch my breath. How could you permit such peeping and prying? In a sealed chamber, the wind cannot pass; at the profound gate, it is difficult to set foot.
Nevertheless, though this be so, a single point of luminous spirit penetrates the universe; how can it be confined to West India or Caoxi?
The third case: When Yunyan was traveling in the mountains, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"Since there are no companions who are not already traveling with us, how could our expedient means fail to be of our own house? It requires neither seeing with the eyes nor hearing with the ears;
it is far superior to merely following sounds and chasing forms. Tell me, where lies the skillful means for guiding others?"

Yunmen Wenyan once went mountain-viewing with Yaoshan (When the path ends at the water’s edge, sit and watch the clouds arise). A sound rang out from the sword at Yaoshan’s waist (How many are there who truly know?).

Yunmen asked, “What thing is making that sound? (The mouth is the gate of calamity. Yaoshan then drew his sword and made a motion to strike him across the face (In dealing with others, he did not spare even his own eyebrows).
The Master said: "Chan Master Weiyen of Yaoshan in Lizhou was a successor of Shitou. He ascended the hall and said: 'The Patriarch taught only that we must protect [the mind].
If greed, anger, or delusion arise, you must strictly guard against them; do not allow them to cause disturbance.
If you wish to know the withered tree or the stone, you must take up this burden; truly, there are no branches or leaves to be found. Although it is thus, you should still further apply yourself."

Look for yourself. You must not cease your speech. I shall now speak these words for you to reveal that state which is beyond speech—that original condition devoid of ears, eyes, and other such features.
Once, while traveling with Yunyan through the mountains, the sound of a sword clinking at his waist reached the Master's ears. Yunyan asked him about it;
the Master drew the blade and made a sweeping motion across his own throat. Later, Dongshan brought this up to instruct the assembly, saying, "Look at him."
Yaoshan laid his body across [the path] for this very matter. If people of the present day wish to clarify the matter of the "Upward Direction," they must first realize this meaning;

only then will it be attained. Linquanzi, look closely: you all must keep this in mind and apply it throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, never missing the moment nor failing the opportunity, so that it is seen, spoken, and applied, wondrously harmonizing and encompassing all, rather than being merely a matter of words.
[This is] settled. If you do not believe it, try listening to the sound of the cheers from Touzi Jueguo and Liaole as they come. The verse says:

The great garuḍa passes through the celestial lake without a companion (always traveling alone, always walking alone). The lion leads its cub, leaving no trace behind (all other beasts hide their tracks).
Truly difficult to compare. When Kunlun commits an offense, he returns to his path (save your straw sandals well).
With one roar, he swallows the clouds and ten thousand forms scatter (only then do you know the Great Mouth; he never looked at human sentiment).
The Master said: "In the Northern Ocean there is a fish; its name is Kun. As for the size of the Kun, one knows not how many thousands of li it is.
It transforms and becomes a bird; its name is Peng. As for the back of the Peng, one knows not how many thousands of li it is.
When it rises in a rage and flies, its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky. This bird, with the movement of the sea, is about to migrate to the Southern Ocean. As for the Southern Ocean—"
It is a celestial pond. Those with wisdom may attain understanding through this metaphor.

I wish to cause the ocean-like nature-sea of the white-robed disciples to be vast and expansive, so that they may soar and cry out with freedom, unbound by the burning house of the three realms and unhindered by the fetters of the delusive objects of the six sense-dusts.
Thus, the old man Yaoshan, through the occasion of raising his son, has bestowed his full heart and effort for their salvation, speaking directly—
Having reached the Kunlun heights, one also seeks to return home. It is not that one does not see the Way: the green mountains constantly lift their feet, yet the white sun does not shift its wheel.
At this very moment, how should one thoroughly comprehend it? *Du!* Though it be so, drawing a sword is difficult when it must be returned to its scabbard.
"Do not let old Mañjuśrī be put to shame.

The fourth case: Daowu deeply instructed the assembly, saying, "To seek out the hidden and probe the profound is to treat the light as laborious and the heavy as a burden. To present [the truth] face-to-face, I do not decline to serve you. For...
Is this the wondrous application of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), or is it the supernatural power itself that is wondrous? Let those with the eye of discernment examine this.
A monk once asked Dao Wu, "What is the Master’s deepest place? (It is not something that can be known by wisdom; it is not something that can be recognized by consciousness.

Dao Wu descended from his meditation seat and performed a woman’s bow, saying, "Thank you for coming from afar; there is nothing to offer as a reception" (expressing gratitude for your profound courtesy).
The Master said: "The First Patriarch, the Great Being Bodhidharma, declared: 'I have come to this land to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings.
One flower opens into five petals; the fruition will naturally be accomplished. Under the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi, the lineage split into two."
The first was Nanyue Huairang; the second was Qingyuan Xingsi. Below Huairang, the lineage further divided into two:
Guiyang and Linji. Below Xingsi, it likewise divided into three: Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan. Thus, the single stream of Caoxi is now divided into five.
This corresponds to the prophetic saying that "one flower shall bear five petals. Great!
The Dharma transmitted to each [school] is fundamentally no different; it is only because they have established their own lineages that their pedagogical arrangements differ.
This prostration performed by the woman is the specific functional application (*jìyòng*) of the Mí-yǎng tradition.

That school possesses ninety-seven types of "perfect circles" (*yuánxiàng*), which are further subsumed under six categories: first, the perfect circle; second, the ocean of meaning; third, the dark trigger; fourth, the manifold...

Regarding the study of characters: fifth is intentional speech; sixth is silent discourse. Now, in Daowu’s response, he employs a dark mechanism of silent discourse to present [the truth] face-to-face.
This is a profound and mysterious pivot, handed over with both hands. Do not say it is remote, desolate, and difficult to perceive;
viewed through the correct eye, such claims have already become a leakage. Since he has been seen through by bystanders, to reward him would be as appropriate as to punish him.
This is it. This is Tiantou’s own knowledge of where he has descended. The verse says:

The black dragon lies coiled in the sea, auspicious clouds rise high (thoroughly without dependence, one knows how to turn the body). Looking in the four directions, all return to the source; ten thousand streams flow as tides (all emerge from this very place).
A wooden man comes to ask about the affairs of the Western Palace (one must not recklessly transmit news). He turns his grace back upon the Eastern Garden with a single peach.
(When folding my hands to offer this gift, I am moved by your profound kindness. How many can truly know the flavor within?
The Master said: "Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. The principles of nature correspond to one another without obstruction.
You must stand atop the highest mountain peak, ensuring your nostrils reach the heavens; you must walk upon the deepest ocean floor, grasping the very point beneath your feet."
It is not merely that the six gates are closed; one can further leave no trace upon the four crossroads. If you understand it thus, what depth or shallowness could possibly be measured?
Since all conditions have been stilled in this way, why worry that the myriad streams will not flow into the tide?

One may gaze afar from the four distant quarters and attach oneself to this single school as much as one pleases. Although the palace is surrounded by a double enclosure and sight and hearing are difficult to penetrate, [the truth remains manifest].

The wooden woman and stone man have long conveyed news of their condition. If you would grant even a slight descent of the imperial decree, what harm would there be in making an exception for these times?
Since you have already granted me the pouring forth of your heart’s core, do not again lose your head by mistaking it for a reflection. Do you understand?

When the beautiful lady gazes at the moon and offers her prayers, how many know of the rustling of her silken skirt? Since Liu Lang has departed, spring has no master; the fruit ripens and its fragrance wafts abroad.
"To whom was this given?

The fifth case: Yanguan addressed the assembly, saying, "Discern the field from its sprouts; recognize the person through their words. Only when the present moment is fully exhausted does one finally achieve realization. From here on...
From the shallow to the profound—how can one probe and extract [the essence]?
Yunyan’s first meeting with Yaoshan is cited: (As for "Teacher," he simply prostrated; as for "Dharma," he sought it everywhere. Yaoshan asked, "Where have you come from? (One must not fail to ask.)
[The Master] said, "It is said that Baizhang came [to the assembly]. (Much talk is not as good as a little reality. [The Master] asked, "What words did Baizhang have?
(He profoundly exhausted the subtle principle. [The Master] said, "At times he would say: 'A single phrase contains all a hundred flavors. (This is like asking for more salt and vinegar on top of it.

[The Master] asked, "'Salty is the flavor of salt; bland is the flavor of blandness; neither salty nor bland is the ordinary flavor. What is the phrase that contains all a hundred flavors? (Please harmonize with me.)
(Try to taste it and swallow it. He said, "What can you do about birth and death right before your eyes? (He pats his nephew to frighten the child.
[The Master] said, "There is no birth and death before my eyes" (a blatant lie). He said, "Twenty years at Baizhang, and you still cannot eliminate your worldly airs" (capturing him alive).
He asked again, "Brother Hai, what further Dharma do you preach? (discerning the source in detail. He replied, "Sometimes I say to 'go beyond the three phrases.'"
[The Master] said, "What is the use of so much external gathering and grasping? He replied, "Three thousand miles away, I am glad there is no connection.
[The Master] asked again, "What further Dharma do you speak? He said, "Sometimes, after the assembly has finished descending from the hall, he calls out to the assembly once more.
The assembly turns their heads. [The Master] said, "It is like sifting sand to find gold; the entire hall is full of Chan monks."
Yunmen then said, "What is this? (Even the thousand sages do not recognize it. Xiangyan asked, "Why did you not say so earlier? (The busy do not understand; those who understand are not busy.
At these words, Xiangyan attained realization (only then did he believe that the meditation cushion was no ordinary thing).
The Master said: "Chan Master Tan-zhou Yun-yan Tan-sheng relied upon Baizhang Hai for twenty years, yet their karmic conditions did not harmonize.
Later, he went to Yaoshan. Yaoshan questioned him as before, and Yun-yan answered as before, until the final question: 'What is this place?'"
Mount said, "Why did you not speak thus sooner? Today, because of you, I have been able to see Elder Hai.
At these words, Yan was suddenly enlightened; he then prostrated himself. Only then could one say that there is not much to it—it is merely a matter of saving a little effort.

Their authority is like the rare phoenix feather; how could they have known that all phenomena are established from the groundless root? Form arises before substance; names emerge from the nameless.
None can compare them to those who crossed the shifting sands to the West or came to Shaoshi in the East, attaining the skin and marrow, and transmitting the Dharma and the Mind.

Non-dual and indivisible, for there is no distinction and no interruption. Why must one gaze at the mountains by day, play with the waters before the cliffs, contemplate flowers within the balustrade, or peck at the trees?

The Master said: "Chan Master Wenyuan of Guangfeng Monastery on Mount Yunmen in Shaoyou was a native of Jiaxing. He left the household life under the Vinaya Master Zhicheng;

Since this monk had already penetrated the "phrase of the Dharma-body," Yunmen was compelled to respond with all his heart, saying: "Hide yourself within the Northern Dipper."
It is not that I am teaching you to look upward and fail to reach it; nor is it that I am teaching you to seek and fail to find it.

"It rains. The Master said:

At that time, one must maintain the mind. Those who seek this profoundly will weep; they will wander in hesitation.
Ultimately, how could the news of that which transcends words and cuts off thought ever be grasped through casual or easy means? Have you not seen it said: "Precisely because it is most clear"?

Those who obtain it find their heads light and their eyes clear; those who lose it feel their hearts anxious and their bellies burning hot. One can well imagine the people of Aparagoyānī.

"Head. This refers to the question posed to the Magistrate of Huángchéng. This question and this answer cannot be understood through intentional effort, nor can they be known through a state of non-mind.

"The path that points upward is one where the thousand sages do not travel; in the mere moment of hesitation, one loses one's life."

One loses one’s life. Thus we know that to direct the mind [toward such things] is already a deviation; to take a single step is already an error. If one falls into a pit or a ditch, what cause for resentment is there?

One ought instead to be filled with awe and trepidation, folding one’s wings in reverence as one looks up to your virtue with earnest devotion. Gazing afar at the Purple Palace enshrouded in mist, waiting to behold the Dragon Pavilion welcoming auspicious omens;

within the deep inner chambers and the guarded curtains, where all is silent and the incense has faded—there is no room for leisurely wandering, nor can one afford even a moment’s breath. If one were to breathe...

Within a single breath, the journey spans ten thousand miles. If one is willing to forget conditions and reach the Holy Way, there is no road within the midst that can separate one from the dust. The verse says:

The deep palace and forbidden halls are separated by layered gates (the ninefold deep and secret place). The curtains are still, and from the eaves and rafters purple qi descends (no outsiders are permitted).

Know that the moss-covered ground does not permit the arrival of court messengers (one must not recklessly transmit news). When family members point out the way, do not hesitate (you must be thorough;

The Master said: "The Way of our Buddha is subtle and profound, difficult to clarify. Though the six gates are open, the four ministers stand with hands folded.

To attain it is to move freely and without obstruction; to lose it is to encounter hindrance at every turn. If one lets go, even tiles and rubble emit light; if one holds fast, even pure gold loses its luster.
How much more so in the deep inner palace and the forbidden halls, further separated by layered screens—it would be difficult indeed to traverse them by sight or hearing."
Truly, there is nothing that can serve as a metaphor for the Way of the Sage; it cannot be compared through names or words.

Yet, when the curtains are drawn in stillness within the eaves and rafters, it becomes even more difficult to approach. When the moon sinks behind the courtyard buildings, who would dare to draw near?

For those who walk this Path, what face could they show, and by what name could they be reached? One can only revere them from afar while looking down upon them with disdain; yet, once face-to-face— [The text ends abruptly.]
It is better to hear the name; this allows one to clarify the ultimate truth within the conventional. Only by abandoning phenomena can one then attain the principle.
You must examine and reflect with meticulous care; do not be negligent or act in haste and emptiness. Although these words may be harsh to the ear, they are ultimately loyal counsel.

Who would resent that the mossy ground does not allow passage for the Imperial Court? I pray that the silken edicts have not yet been issued and the gracious summons has not descended from afar. Though my family members point the way...
The Dark Portal: Those who understand rarely encounter the clear mirror. Disciples of the ancestral school must avoid hesitation; sharp-witted monks must examine things with great care.

The ninety-first case: Yangshan thrusts his spade into the ground and addresses the assembly, saying:

[The Master] said, "So it is.

Mount [Shishuang] clarifies the matter of one’s own fundamental allotment through the family style of that fundamental allotment.
